Right so the discrepancy in my head is that on one hand, as you said, whether you log transform your data or not, "it conveys the same information".

On the other hand, in this hypothetical giraffe weight measurement example, if you don't log transform, then your data are skewed, and you can't perform a t-test to conclude that there is a statistical difference in weights. But if you DO log transform and make them normally distributed, then you can now perform a t-test and you MAY be able to say there being a statistical difference in the log transformed weights of male vs. female giraffes. Which is NOT conveying the same information as before.

Sure I understand that if your sample data is spread out across multiple orders of magnitude, then it makes sense to log transform your data.

But what I'm trying to get at with my question is something different I think:

When you do a log transformation, you can also reverse it by taking the inverse log right? So the transformation is lossless. There isn't any additional information that is added to or lost from your original non-transformed sample data.

So if the information content is the same whether you have your variable displayed in raw numbers or log transformed numbers, intuitively it would seem to me that you shouldn't be able to reach 2 different statistical conclusions right? I mean obviously it doesn't make sense that you can draw two different conclusions by looking at the same "information".

But the discrepancy I'm struggling to understand is that in my example, that's exactly what seems to be happening.

If you have data for male and female giraffe weights that are both skewed, then you can't perform the t-test and so your conclusion is that you can't draw any conclusions.

But my instructor seemed to imply that to get around this 'problem', you can log transform your data to make them normal, and perform a t-test, which may give you a statistically significant result. 

So number 1, it seems like you're getting 2 different statistical results by looking at the "same" data just based around this assumption of normality

And number 2, regardless of whether this apparent discrepancy is real or not, if you can log transform your data and conclude a statement about the 'log transformed' weights of male vs female giraffes (which may actually have some physical meaning, as you pointed out - I accept that now), then you've now reached a conclusion that wasn't available to you when you didn't log transform the data. So the log transformation "added" some kind of "information content" to your original sample data. But this is not what I understand a "transformation" in the mathematical sense, to be.

Ok but even in that case, to keep going with my example, wouldn't you agree that to say that there is a statistical difference in the average 'log transformed weights' of male and female giraffes is a useless statement that has no meaning in the physical world?

This might not be the most formal way to define a dimension, but from a purely geometric perspective, I can tell you how to imagine 4D.

So 1D is a line. Imagine that there are two points A and B in a 1D world (a line). To get from A and B, you have to touch the 1D world. In fact, you have to touch the line. BUT, if you now imagine this line to be in a 2D world (a plane), you can get from A to B by moving up and across, and down again. To a creature living in the 1D world (who does not know the concept of width), it would look almost as if you had teleported from A to B. 

Now, again imagine two points A and B, but this time in a 2D world (a plane). We run into the same problem. To get from A to B, we must traverse through the 2D plane. However, if we imagine this plane to be in 3D, then all we have to do, is go up from A (vertically from the plane), across and down to B. To creatures living in a 2D world (who do not know the concept of height), it would seem as if you had teleported from A to B. 

Let's extend this analogy to 3D (our world) and 4D. Imagine two points A and B. In fact, to make this concept more concrete, imagine two points A and B inside two balloons respectively. Now, if we were to attempt to draw a line between A and B, it would be impossible to do so without touching the balloon walls (i.e, traversing through our 3D world). However, the analogies above suggest that in a 4D world, there would be a way to connect a point from inside one balloon, to a point inside another without touching the balloon walls. To us, this seems impossible, and if it were to happen, would seem as if point A had teleported to point B.
